title: Oankar made all
hookLine: from the One came Brahma and all creation

lines: A MUG, A POTTER, A HILLSIDE.
THE OANKAR STARTS AT THE END.
cards: Pick up the nearest object, a mug, say. Someone shaped it, someone fired it, someone dug the clay. The clay came out of a hillside, and the hillside came out of something older still.
Follow any made thing back, and the trail gets long and strange very fast. The Oankar starts at the far end of that trail. Its opening lines don't begin with a letter to learn.
They begin with where everything came from.

teach.b: Here is the opening of the Oankar, in paraphrase. From Oankar, Brahma came to be. Brahma kept Oankar in his mind.

teach.h: THE MOUNTAINS, THE AGES, THE VEDAS.
teach.b: From Oankar came the mountains and the ages. From Oankar the Vedas were made. Remember who Nanak is speaking to, in the tradition: a pandit, a teacher of the Vedas.

teach.h: THE PANDIT'S OWN WORLD, TRACED BACK.
teach.b: So the poem opens in the pandit's own world: Brahma, the creator in his own tradition; the Vedas, the scriptures he taught. Nanak dismisses none of them. He traces each back to its source.
Brahma came from the One, and remembered the One. The mountains, the long ages, the holy books themselves: from Oankar.
It's the move we watched in the Sidh Gosht, using the other person's language, now in a schoolroom instead of on a mountain. And it's the move the mug made a minute ago.
Whatever is in front of you, a scripture, a mountain, a cup, follow it back far enough and the poem says you arrive at one place. Notice the word kept in that second line.
In the poem, even Brahma, the creator, is a rememberer.

teach.h: NOTHING IS A STRANGER TO IT.
teach.b: That matters for an ordinary day: if everything comes from the One, nothing in front of you is a stranger to it.
Look back over this week's lines: the name in the breath, yoga in daily life, the yogis bowed, answer kindly, keep talking, letters of wisdom.
And now the root under all of them: from the one.

how: The Guru Granth Sahib opens with Ik Oankar, the One Creator; the Oankar in Raga Ramkali opens by tracing all creation back to that One.

o: a letter children learn to write first
the first word of the pandit's lesson
everything traced back to the One

games.q: what's inside Oankar made all — tap the pairs.
p: made from Oankar, the poem says

s: the Oankar opens by dismissing the pandit's world
it names Brahma and the Vedas and traces each back to the One.
in the poem, Brahma himself remembers Oankar
Brahma kept Oankar in his mind.
the Oankar's opening begins with a spelling lesson
it begins with where everything came from.

games.q: you're answering a pandit who teaches the Vedas. how does the Oankar open?
o: by saying the Vedas are wrong.
by tracing Brahma, the mountains and the Vedas back to the One.
by leaving his scriptures out entirely.
games.why: from Oankar, Brahma; from Oankar, the mountains and the ages; from Oankar, the Vedas. the poem meets him in his own world.

practice: Choose something within reach, a cup, a pencil, a slice of bread, and follow it back one slow step at a time: who made it, what it was made of, where that came from, and before that.

Don't hurry to an answer at the end; just notice how many hands and how much earth are in one small thing. If you pray, let the trail end in the One the Oankar names; if not, rest in the wonder of the trail itself.

wordCard.voice: Oankar made all. The poem's opening: from Oankar came Brahma, the mountains, the ages and the Vedas. Today's word.

orig.note: Oankar: a name for the One, and the word each of the poem's opening lines begins with.

carryVoice: Your line: from the one. Brahma, the mountains, the Vedas, a mug: one source. That's the week.

sources.ref: Ramkali Mahala 1, Dakhni Oankar, opening ('oankar brahma utpat'), Ang 929
